claim: Eliminated the state tax on diapers and baby supplies.
record: HB152 (2025) exempts diapers, baby formula and related items from the state sales tax only, from Sep 1, 2025 through Aug 31, 2028 (temporary). Sponsor was Rep. Neil Rafferty (D) with co-sponsors not including Marques. The House passed it unanimously. Overstates his role and the permanence.

claim: Marques voted for a 67% gas and diesel tax increase.
record: Marques did vote for the 2019 Rebuild Alabama fuel-tax increase (al.com via Wikipedia). The 67% figure was not checked against the act's rate schedule.

text: Corporate and trade PACs gave in 2024, including Regions Financial, Truist, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, Ernst & Young, American Crystal Sugar, Volkert (DVAHC) PAC and National Beer Wholesalers ($5,000 each). In the 2024 primary and runoff, the crypto-industry super PAC Protect Progress spent about $2.39M supporting him. PAC money is 63% of his 2025–26 contributions.

Pro-Israel PAC money: AIPAC PAC gave $5,000 directly (Oct 2024) and DMFI PAC $1,000 (Sep 2024). DMFI PAC also made independent expenditures for him in 2024. Track AIPAC lists a $63,235 career pro-Israel total.

claim: Voters in the district have lacked chances to connect with their representative for about a decade.
record: A Rogers in-person town hall in 2017 is documented, and his House site offers telephone town-hall sign-up; no 2025–2026 in-person town hall was found. The claim is broadly consistent with the record found but overstates it if telephone events count.

claim: Initiated and oversaw the creation of the U.S. Space Force, with bipartisan support.
record: With Rep. Jim Cooper (D) he proposed a Space Corps in 2017; it passed the House but died in the Senate. Similar language was later enacted to create the Space Force (FY2020 NDAA). He was a lead originator, but enactment also required the Senate and the administration.

claim: Was a practicing attorney and small business owner in Calhoun County.
record: Opened a law firm in Anniston after 1991 (documented). No separate small business was identified in the sources reviewed.

text: His House campaign took $721,704.50 from non-party committees (PACs) in 2025–26 and $7.93M (43.5%) of $18.24M raised across the 11 cycles retrieved (2004–2014, 2018–2026); a business-vs-ideological split isn't available. 1819 News, citing OpenSecrets, reported Lockheed Martin-affiliated individuals and its PAC were his largest contributor in the 2022 cycle ($60,750) while it competed for a missile-defense contract (Next Generation Interceptor) he urged be accelerated; it reported the same for a Ukraine missile system in Jan. 2023.

claim: In 2014 he said he would serve only 10 years in Congress.

said.where: 2014 campaign (as reported by Alabama Reflector and Wikipedia)

record: Rated as a promise against the record: he sought a sixth term in 2024 and is now seeking a seventh in 2026. U.S. Term Limits accused him of breaking a pledge. He said he had received clarity from God to run again.

text: Business and trade PAC money every documented cycle. claim: Expanding Medicaid would cover "more than 154,000 working Alabamians."

said.where: campaign Priorities page (item 4, as of access date)

record: Families USA (March 2026) estimates about 154,842 low-income adults could enroll under expansion after removing an estimated 36% who would lose coverage under new federal work-reporting rules. Alabama Arise cites 'up to 155,000.' The figure matches these advocacy estimates, but the source does not count how many are 'working'; it is the number expected to remain enrolled under work reporting.

claim: Alabama is turning down "roughly $182 million in federal healthcare funding each year."
record: The number matches Families USA's estimate of $181.6 million for 2026, but that figure is state costs and lost savings (uncompensated care, existing Medicaid groups, mental health, inmate inpatient care) that federal expansion money could cover. It is not the total federal expansion funding forgone, which would be larger. The estimate comes from an advocacy group, drawing on PARCA's 2022 study.

claim: Tuberville called residents' concerns about electric bills, water use and harm to communities and the environment "bullcrap."

said.where: first TV ad (as described by ADN)

record: On July 13, 2026, Tuberville said of the claim that data centers will ruin the climate: 'bull crap.' In the same remarks he blamed opposition on Chinese social-media influence. The recorded remark was about the climate claim. It was not shown to be about electric bills or water, and on July 23 he said he understands why Alabamians might be hesitant.

claim: "No one has ever — ever — questioned my being an Alabama resident for my entire life."
record: Records support Alabama residency: he and his wife have claimed a homestead exemption on their Mountain Brook home continuously since buying it in 2010. But after leaving the Senate he worked from ArentFox Schiff's Washington office, and more than 25 FEC receipts and a PAC record list that D.C. address. Lagniappe was questioning his records when he made the statement. He declined to share state tax receipts.

text: Business and trade-group PAC money in his Senate career, e.g., Charter Communications, Comcast/NBCUniversal, Lockton, National Apartment Association and American Institute of CPAs PACs ($5,000 each, 2020 cycle). Other-committee receipts totaled $875,252 (2017–18) and $1,943,850 (2019–20), a mix of business, labor, party and ideological PACs. In 2017 the Highway 31 super PAC, 'predominantly funded' by Senate Majority PAC, spent more than $4 million against his opponent; SMP's own donors were not retrieved. No corporate contributions were reported in his 2026 state filings. His reported PAC money there is mostly labor, party and Democratic-politician PACs.

FEC-itemized pro-Israel PAC contributions in the 2019–20 cycle: NORPAC $5,150, JACPAC $5,000, Friends of Israel PAC $5,000, DMFI PAC $3,000, Pro-Israel America PAC $1,000 ($19,150 total). Track AIPAC has no entry for him, and 2017–18 pro-Israel PAC itemization could not be retrieved.

claim: "My wife and I, Suzanne, moved here over 25 years ago."
record: He became Auburn's head coach in 1999, so he first moved to Alabama more than 25 years before 2025. But the record shows long periods elsewhere: head coach at Texas Tech (2010–12) and Cincinnati (2013–16); in a 2017 ESPN video he said he had retired to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida; his Florida beach home got a Florida homestead exemption in 2018; he voted in Florida in November 2018 and registered to vote in Alabama on March 28, 2019.

claim: "Unlike Doug Jones, Coach has also accepted ZERO PAC (political action committee) money."

said.where: campaign manager Jordan Doufexis statement to Alabama Reflector

record: The same Alabama Reflector review of his state filings found about $10,000 in PAC contributions (Diversified Gas & Oil PAC $2,500; Travelers PAC $2,500; Home Depot PAC $5,000) plus in-kind PAC contributions (BANKPAC $3,600; Truk PAC $7,200; Alabama Farm PAC nearly $3,000). In September 2026 he took $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC. (His campaign had told reporters in January 2026 it was not accepting PAC money.)

claim: Opponents' education plan "kicks tens of thousands of children out of the school of their choice."
record: More than 34,000 students were approved for CHOOSE Act accounts for 2026–27, so 'tens of thousands' matches program size. But Jones said on July 29–30, 2026: 'The kids that are in there now, let them finish, but quit taking applications.' He later vowed to 'stop the CHOOSE Act in its tracks' without saying current students would lose funding.

text: Eight investors sued him, partner John David Stroud and their TS Capital entities in federal court in 2012, alleging securities fraud. Stroud pleaded guilty to criminal securities fraud and got 10 years. Tuberville was never charged (investigators said he was also a victim) and settled with the plaintiffs under sealed terms on Oct. 8, 2013.

Reported about 130 stock and option trades from Jan.–May 2021 (worth $894,000 to $3.5 million) after the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline. His office said he was unaware of the trades, filed the report, and paid the late-filing penalty. The Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the Senate Ethics Committee on July 29, 2021.
status: Late-filing penalty paid; no public Senate Ethics action found

text: Business and trade-group PAC money in his federal career: e.g., Nucor, Raytheon Technologies, FedEx, Boeing, U.S. Steel, Vulcan Materials, Marathon Petroleum, Home Depot and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama PACs ($5,000 each, 2020 cycle); Cadence Bank, Regions, Endo Pharmaceuticals and many agriculture trade PACs (2024 cycle). claim: In 2010 he defeated a six-term Democratic incumbent to win his Alabama House seat.
record: He defeated Democrat Terry Spicer in 2010 (9,754–5,383). Spicer served District 91 from 1998 to 2010 — three four-year terms, not six.

claim: In Trump's first term, working-class wages grew faster than elite wages for the first time in fifty years.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — The Economy (claim 6)

record: Atlanta Fed data showed the lowest-paid quarter of workers getting larger percentage raises than the top quarter since 2015, a trend that began before his term and that CBS tied largely to state minimum-wage increases. No source was found for the 'first time in fifty years' part.

claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill gives working families and small business owners a real tax cut.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — The Economy (claim 7)

record: The law cut taxes, including new deductions for tips and overtime. But CBO's analysis of the House-passed version found household resources would generally fall for the lowest-income households (largely due to Medicaid and SNAP cuts) and rise for middle and top households.

text: Arrested in April 2014 on two felony perjury counts and two counts of making false statements, tied to a Lee County grand jury investigation of House Speaker Mike Hubbard. He had been recorded pressuring primary opponent Josh Pipkin to drop out. A jury found him not guilty on all counts on Oct. 30, 2014. Before trial, the Alabama Supreme Court rejected his challenge to the grand jury and the special prosecutors' appointment (Sept. 2014).

Defend American Jobs, the Republican-side crypto super PAC in the Fairshake network (Fairshake is funded mainly by Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz), spent about $12.2 million supporting him in the 2026 Senate race (nearly $7M through the May primary per Mother Jones). His Senate campaign also took $881,597.83 from non-party PACs through June 30, 2026, but the business share of that couldn't be broken out.
Track AIPAC lists $30,173 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC listed) and their large donors; $0 in pro-Israel independent expenditures.

said.t: Opposed the Fiscal Responsibility Act, saying it would 'saddle Americans with $4 trillion in new debt'; also opposed raising the debt ceiling in 2021. Campaigns in 2026 on reducing the national debt.

did.t: Voted Aye on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), which raised the debt limit by $5 trillion and which CBO estimated would add trillions to deficits over a decade (figures reported range from $2.8T to $3.4T depending on the estimate). The bill also contained spending cuts he supported.
